lead: A manometer measures pressure by balancing it against a liquid column. The rule is simple: in the same continuous fluid at the same level, pressure is the same. Follow the tube from the unknown pressure to the open end. Add ρgh when the path goes down; subtract ρgh when it goes up. This turns a pressure into a height you can see. Manometers check pipe pressure, filter drop and laboratory drafts.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 for gauge pressure and p = ρgh.

sections.h3: Balance a column, read a pressure

blocks.text: A manometer is a transparent tube with a liquid. The unknown pressure pushes one liquid surface. The other surface is open, or held at a known pressure. The liquid settles when the pressure difference is balanced by the weight of the liquid column. The working rule is: in one continuous static fluid, two points at the same horizontal level have the same pressure.

A piezometer is the simplest manometer. It is a vertical tube open at the top, fixed to a pipe. The liquid rises to height h above the pipe centre. Then p = ρgh, where p is gauge pressure at the pipe centre in Pa, ρ is liquid density in kg/m³, g is gravitational acceleration in m/s² and h is height in m. A piezometer needs a liquid, so it cannot measure gas pressure in a pipe. It also needs a tall tube for high pressure.

The U-tube removes these limits. A heavy liquid such as mercury sits in a U. One limb connects to the pipe; the other is open. The pressure in the pipe moves the mercury. The height difference h is the reading. The U-tube can measure gas pressure and higher pressures because mercury is dense.
p_A + ρ_w g h₁ − ρ_Hg g h = p_atm
blocks.where: p_A is the pressure at A; ρ_w and ρ_Hg are the densities of water and mercury; h₁ is the downward water column; h is the upward mercury column; p_atm is the open-end pressure. For gauge pressure, set p_atm = 0.

items: Piezometer. A single vertical tube open to air. It uses the pipe liquid only. p = ρgh. It suits low pressures in liquids, not gases, and not negative gauge pressures that would draw air in.
U-tube manometer. A U-shaped tube with a heavy gauge liquid, often mercury. One limb connects to the point; the other is open. It reads gas or liquid pressure. The height difference is h.

Differential U-tube. Two limbs connect to two points. It reads p₁ − p₂. When both legs have the same liquid above mercury and the tappings are level, p₁ − p₂ = (ρ_Hg − ρ_f) g h. ρ_f is the fluid in the pipes.
Inverted U-tube. A light fluid, such as air or oil, is trapped at the top. It suits small pressure differences between liquids. A heavy fluid would fall and destroy the trapped layer.

Inclined manometer. The tube is tilted at angle θ to the horizontal. The scale reads length L along the tube. The vertical height is h = L sin θ. For the same h, L = h / sin θ, so a small θ gives a long, easy-to-read scale. This is called increased sensitivity.

blocks.text: The manometer equation is not a formula to memorise for each shape. It is a path sum. Use it for any U-tube, inverted tube or inclined tube. Write pressures in Pa. Convert heights to m. Convert densities to kg/m³. Keep the same g for both legs.

items: Start at one end with p_A. Use gauge pressure if the question asks gauge.
Move along one continuous fluid path.
When the path goes down by a vertical height z, add ρgz.
When it goes up by z, subtract ρgz. ρ is the density of the fluid in that part.
At the same horizontal level in the same fluid, cross without adding anything: the pressure is equal.
At an open end, write p_atm. For gauge pressure, put p_atm = 0.
Solve the resulting equation for the unknown.
Check the sign: a pipe pressure above atmosphere must give a positive gauge answer.

blocks.text: The path can start at either end. Starting at the open end is allowed; the signs reverse. If a limb has two fluids, change density at the interface, not at the same-level crossing.

figure.caption: Follow the path from A to the open end: the water column adds pressure, the same-level mercury crossing changes nothing, and the mercury column subtracts pressure. The open end sits at atmospheric pressure.

spec.title: Manometer equation path
spec.aria: The manometer equation follows the tube from point A down through water, across mercury and up to the open end at atmospheric pressure.

examples.question: A horizontal water pipe has a U-tube mercury manometer. The water column from the pipe centre to the left mercury surface is h₁ = 0.40 m. The right mercury surface is h = 0.15 m above the left mercury surface and is open to atmosphere. ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, ρ_Hg = 13,600 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find the gauge pressure in the pipe in Pa and kPa.
steps: Take gauge pressure at the open right surface as 0.
Start at the pipe centre A with pressure p_A.
Go down the water column h₁ = 0.40 m: pressure rises by 1000 × 9.81 × 0.40 = 3,924 Pa.
Cross the mercury at the left-surface level. The right limb at that level has the same pressure.
Go up mercury h = 0.15 m: pressure falls by 13,600 × 9.81 × 0.15 = 20,012.4 Pa.
At the open surface, gauge pressure is 0. So p_A + 3,924 − 20,012.4 = 0.
examples.answer: The gauge pressure in the pipe is 16,088.4 Pa, which is about 16.09 kPa.
examples.check:
rw = 1000
rhg = 13600
g = 9.81
h1 = 0.40
h = 0.15
p_pa = rhg*g*h - rw*g*h1
print(round(p_pa, 1))
print(round(p_pa/1000, 2))

traps: Down add, up subtract, from the starting pressure. Reversing the path reverses every sign; do not mix.
Use gauge zero at an open end for gauge pressure. Do not add 101.3 kPa unless absolute pressure is asked.
A fluid contributes ρgh only along its own continuous column. Crossing at the same level in the same fluid adds nothing.
In an inclined tube the scale reads L, not h. Convert with h = L sin θ.
In a differential manometer, cancel the common fluid only when both legs have the same fluid and the tappings are at the same level; otherwise use the full path.

quiz.q: State the rule for pressure at two points on the same horizontal level in one continuous static fluid.
Why can a piezometer not be used to measure gas pressure in a pipe?
quiz.a: It is open at the top; gas would escape and no stable liquid column would form.

quiz.q: A U-tube mercury manometer is open to atmosphere. The left mercury surface is 0.25 m below the right. The water column from the pipe centre to the left mercury surface is 0.30 m. ρw = 1000 kg/m³, ρHg = 13,600 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find the gauge pressure.
For a differential U-tube with both legs filled with the same liquid above mercury and level tappings, show p₁ − p₂ = (ρHg − ρw)gh.
quiz.a: Start at 1, add water down, subtract mercury up h, subtract water up the other leg. The common water terms cancel, leaving p₁ − p₂ = (ρHg − ρw)gh.

quiz.q: What does an inclined manometer improve, and by what factor does the reading grow?
quiz.a: It improves sensitivity. For tube angle θ, h = L sin θ, so L = h / sin θ; the reading grows as θ becomes small.

quiz.q: Why does an inverted U-tube use a light fluid, not mercury?
quiz.a: The light fluid must stay at the top. Mercury is dense and would fall through the liquid, destroying the trapped column; a light fluid gives a measurable h for small Δp.

quiz.q: What gauge pressure is assigned to an open end of a manometer?
quiz.a: Zero gauge; the absolute pressure there is p_atm.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial plants use differential-pressure transmitters with diaphragm seals instead of glass U-tubes, but the same ρgh balance is inside the calibration. Search for "manometer equation", "differential pressure transmitter" and "inclined manometer sensitivity".
